title: Artificial Intelligence in Education, Bridging Community Gap: A Phenomenological Approach
extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence in education might help reduce educational disparities between under-resourced and better-resourced communities in Nigeria. The study is motivated by persistent inequities linked to unequal funding, insecurity, corruption, resource shortages, weak infrastructure, and teacher shortages. Its core research questions ask about teachers’ lived experiences with AI in education, the role of AI in reducing educational disparities, and the problems and opportunities involved in adopting AI-based educational tools in under-resourced communities.

The study uses a phenomenological qualitative design. Data were collected through online, in-depth semi-structured interviews with 15 purposively selected senior secondary public school teachers in Nigeria who had knowledge of AI in education. Thematic analysis produced three major themes: learning assistance, quality education, and infrastructural deficiency. Teachers described AI tools such as virtual tutors, adaptive learning platforms, and automated grading systems, emphasizing their potential for personalized learning, targeted support, improved feedback, and more equitable access to educational resources.

The study context is public secondary education in Nigeria, especially under-resourced communities. Although the stated population was all public secondary school teachers in Nigeria, the actual sample was 15 senior secondary teachers selected based on availability. Interviews were conducted online and lasted about thirteen minutes. The paper focuses on teachers’ perceptions rather than direct measurement of student outcomes or experimental testing of specific AI interventions.

The paper concludes that AI has strong perceived potential to improve learning assistance and educational quality and to help bridge community-level educational gaps by personalizing instruction and expanding access to quality resources. At the same time, participants identified major barriers including poor internet infrastructure, limited funding, lack of teacher support and training, insecurity, corruption, data privacy concerns, and possible reductions in social interaction. The author argues that AI-based technologies could promote more equitable education in underserved Nigerian communities if these implementation challenges are addressed.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic class of AI-based educational systems including virtual tutors, adaptive learning platforms, and automated grading systems that provide personalized instruction, feedback, and performance monitoring.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studied teachers' perceptions of using AI-based educational tools in Nigerian under-resourced secondary schools to provide learning assistance, personalized learning, quality education, and progress tracking.

findings.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews, teachers reported that AI-based tools such as virtual tutors, adaptive learning platforms, and automated grading systems could provide learning assistance through personalized instruction and individualized support. The study identified 'learning assistance' as a core theme from interviews with 15 public secondary school teachers in under-resourced Nigerian communities; no quantitative effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions from semi-structured interviews about learning assistance and personalized learning

findings.finding_summary: Teachers perceived that AI could improve the quality of education in underserved communities by tailoring instruction, tracking student progress, and enabling earlier intervention for struggling students. This conclusion emerged as the 'quality education' theme in a phenomenological study of 15 teachers, with no quantitative outcome metrics reported.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions from semi-structured interviews about education quality improvement and disparity reduction

findings.finding_summary: Teachers identified major implementation barriers alongside potential benefits: infrastructural deficiency, lack of high-speed internet, limited school funding, insufficient teacher training, insecurity, corruption, data privacy concerns, and possible reduction in social interaction and critical thinking. These mixed findings came from thematic analysis of interviews with 15 teachers; no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Teacher perceptions from semi-structured interviews about implementation challenges and opportunities

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative phenomenological study based on semi-structured interviews with 15 teachers, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation. The paper reports perception-based thematic findings without direct student outcome measures or causal identification.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports promising but perception-based benefits and substantial implementation challenges, with no quantitative effect sizes or direct measured impacts on student learning. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.
